generatedProse.concept-context: At Cardiff Met, as at any university, one rule governs everything. Whatever you submit for assessment must show your own understanding and judgement. Because a chatbot predicts likely wording rather than understanding your topic, its answer is not your understanding, so handing it in as your own breaks that rule. Cardiff Met's Academic Handbook is clear that your assignment brief decides whether, and how, you may use AI. If the brief does not say AI is allowed, treat it as not allowed, and ask your tutor if you are unsure. Cardiff Met sets out three categories of AI use - no AI expected, AI acknowledged, and AI embedded - and your brief tells you which applies. The next lesson works through them.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two psychology students who each use a chatbot while writing up a study.

{{learner-a}} types the question, reads the fluent answer, and pastes it into the write-up with a few words changed. It sounded expert, so {{learner-a}} submitted it as their own. But the brief never said AI was allowed, and the paragraph shows the tool's wording, not {{learner-a}}'s understanding. Both the rule and the brief have been broken.

{{learner-b}} checks the brief first to see whether AI is allowed and how. {{learner-b}} then uses the tool only to get unstuck, rewrites the idea from their own understanding, and makes sure the finished work is theirs to explain and defend. The submitted work shows {{learner-b}}'s judgement, not the tool's.

Both students used the same chatbot. Only {{learner-b}} kept the one rule: what you submit must be your own understanding, and the brief decides what is allowed.
generatedProse.summary: Generative AI produces fluent text by predicting likely patterns, not by understanding your topic or looking facts up, so it can be confidently wrong. That is why one rule governs its use at Cardiff Met: whatever you submit must show your own understanding and judgement. Your assignment brief decides whether, and how, you may use AI; if it does not say AI is allowed, treat it as not allowed. You can now explain what the tool is, state that one rule, and see that the brief is where you check. The next lesson looks at the three categories of AI use Cardiff Met sets out: no AI expected, AI acknowledged, and AI embedded.

check.body: Your assignment brief does not mention AI. You ask a chatbot to write a paragraph and you submit it as part of your work. Why is this a problem?

items.text: The brief does not permit AI, and the paragraph is not your own understanding.
It is fine, because the paragraph was well written.
No one will know, as long as you do not tell anyone.
The only problem is that the chatbot was free rather than paid for.

feedback.correct: That's right. If the brief does not say AI is allowed, treat it as not allowed, and submitted work must show your own understanding.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. The brief did not permit AI, and a pasted paragraph is the tool's wording, not your own understanding.
